rejected.title: Improving food security
card: Cutting waste
Food lost on farms, in transport or thrown out at home feeds no one. Less waste means more of the food already grown is eaten.
Caring for soil
Methods such as crop rotation and keeping plant cover protect farmland. Healthy soil keeps growing crops year after year.
Trade
Trade moves food from places with a surplus to places that are short. It helps people get food that their own region cannot grow enough of.
Research
Research can produce new crops, such as ones that cope with drought or salty soil. These let food be grown where it was once hard to farm.
rejected.remember: Waste less, protect soil, trade food and research new crops: each helps secure future supply.

a.q: A town's farms grow plenty of vegetables, but a third rots in storage before it is sold. Which action would best help this problem?
a.why: The food is already grown, so the loss happens after harvest. Cutting waste means more of it gets eaten. Crop rotation protects soil, but it does not stop food rotting in storage.
a.clue: The food is grown. Where does it go missing?

b.q: A small island nation has very little farmland and grows too little rice for its people. Which action would most directly get rice to them?
opts: Importing rice through trade with other countries
Rotating crops on the island's few small farms
Researching drought-tolerant rice for island farms
Cutting rice waste at harvest on island farms
b.why: Trade brings in rice from places that grow more than they need, so it reaches the island's people straight away. Cutting waste, rotating crops or new crop research may help the island's farms, but with so little farmland they still could not grow enough rice.
b.clue: The problem is too little land. Where else could the rice come from?
